title: How I Architected My Astro Portfolio Beyond Pages and Components
excerpt: A source-grounded case study of Folio X: how content contracts, page composition, Project patterns, Components, Layouts, and progressive enhancement work together in a maintainable Astro portfolio.
author: Nguyễn Kim Thu
imageAlt: Layered architecture diagram with content, page composition, project patterns, UI components and layout primitives connected in a vertical Astro system
content:
An Astro portfolio can start as a handful of routes and reusable components. That works until the site grows into several kinds of pages, collections, filters, detail views, editorial content, CMS-managed data, and interactive behaviors. At that point, ‘put everything in src/pages and split large files into components’ is no longer enough of an architecture.

Folio X grew past that point. The current structure is built around a stricter question: who owns each responsibility? Content defines data. Page composition resolves content into approved regions. Project patterns own reusable product-level behavior. Components render smaller UI pieces. Layouts own structural geometry. Scripts progressively enhance the HTML only when a feature exists on the page.

This article explains that architecture from the current develop source. It is not a generic ‘best Astro folder structure’ tutorial. It is a case study of the decisions I made while turning a portfolio into a small content platform that can support projects, labs, products, publications, blog posts, filters, readers, galleries, and CMS editing without letting any one layer take over the whole system.

The problem was not component reuse

Most frontend architecture discussions begin with reuse: extract a card, extract a button, extract a section. Reuse matters, but it was not the main problem I was trying to solve.

The harder problem appeared when the same site had to support very different page shapes while still feeling like one system. A project detail page, a product archive, a blog article, a publication reader, and the home page do not have the same structure. If every route composes its own layout directly, page files become a second design system. If the CMS is allowed to choose arbitrary components, the CMS becomes the design system. If every reusable component also decides where it belongs on a page, component boundaries become unclear.

I needed an architecture where each layer could change for a specific reason:

  • content editors can change content without controlling arbitrary implementation details;
  • page composition can change without rewriting low-level UI components;
  • reusable patterns can own repeated behavior such as card collections or galleries;
  • layout primitives can control spacing and geometry consistently;
  • interactive scripts can remain optional instead of turning every page into a client application.

That led to a layered model rather than a folder tree built only around ‘pages’ and ‘components.’

The architecture in one map

The simplest way to understand the current system is as a data flow. Content does not jump directly into a random component. It moves through explicit contracts until it reaches the HTML that the browser receives.

The important part of the diagram is not the number of boxes. It is the direction of dependency. Higher-level composition is allowed to depend on lower-level rendering primitives. Lower-level components do not reach back upward and decide page structure for themselves.

Layer 1: content is data, not layout code

Astro’s content collections support structured entries loaded from local or remote sources, and schemas can validate the expected shape of each entry. Folio X uses that capability as a contract boundary rather than as a place to hide UI decisions.

The page schema, for example, stores a page slug, metadata, an optional SEO override, a layout template, and a list of approved sections. The schema validates the data before the page builder sees it. That matters because the builder should receive a predictable input shape rather than defensive-checking arbitrary JSON everywhere.

page
├── slug
├── meta
├── seo
└── content
    ├── layout.template
    └── sections[]

This is intentionally different from storing raw HTML for every page or giving the CMS a free-form component picker. The CMS can choose from approved values that the application already understands. The source of truth for the UI remains the application architecture.

Why I did not let the CMS own the UI

A highly dynamic page builder can feel flexible at first. Editors can add blocks, choose variants, reorder everything, and sometimes even enter utility classes. The cost appears later: every new visual option becomes a public data contract that has to remain compatible with old content.

Folio X keeps a narrower boundary. CMS data describes meaningful content and approved presentation choices. Code decides what those choices mean in the actual component system.

For example, the page schema accepts known page templates such as stacked, lead-content, and several lead/navigation combinations. It does not accept an arbitrary Astro component path. That keeps content portable enough to edit while preventing the CMS from becoming a runtime dependency injector.

Layer 2: page composition normalizes content

The page composition layer lives under src/components/pages/. Its job is not to render every visual detail. Its job is to take page data and normalize it into the contracts used by the Project layer.

The home page is a good example. HomePage.astro is intentionally small: it loads the page data and passes it into PageBuilder. The complexity sits in the builder because that is where collection sources, section settings, archive modes, card presentations, and page regions are resolved.

This gives route-level and page-level files a clear responsibility: load the right page data and hand it to composition. They do not need to know how a product card resolves metadata, how a sidebar is laid out, or how a gallery behaves.

The builder is an adapter, not a mega component

PageBuilder.astro is large because it knows how CMS page sections map to application contracts. That does not mean it should own every DOM node. Its main value is adaptation.

For collection sections, it can resolve items from products, projects, labs, blog posts, comics, novels, or the combined publication source. It then maps the CMS card configuration into PCard props. The builder therefore knows that CMS value carousel corresponds to the Project template slider, but the CMS never imports a slider component directly.

This is an important architectural distinction:

LayerQuestion it answers
CMS/contentWhat content and approved presentation choice was selected?
Page builderHow does that data map into application contracts?
Project patternHow does this reusable product-level pattern behave?
ComponentHow is one smaller UI unit rendered?
LayoutHow are elements structurally arranged?

Keeping those questions separate is more useful than trying to minimize the number of files.

Layer 3: PPage owns page-template selection

Once the builder has normalized the page into regions, PPage owns structural template selection. The current source supports five page templates:

  • stacked;
  • lead-content;
  • lead-content-closing;
  • lead-content-navigation;
  • lead-navigation-content.

PPage does not try to infer a template from the children. It receives an explicit template key, selects the corresponding structural template, wraps it in LPage, and passes the page regions down.

That means a page template can answer a structural question such as ‘does the lead appear before navigation?’ without knowing how a card, gallery, CTA, or article is internally rendered.

Page templates control order and section framing

A template such as PageLeadContent separates lead regions from the remaining content, orders them, and decides whether a region should be wrapped by LSection.

The section: false contract is especially useful. It allows a region to opt out of an extra section wrapper when the region already belongs to a larger composition. This prevents page templates from producing unnecessary nested sections merely because the default path wraps everything.

That rule came from repeatedly auditing real DOM output rather than from abstract naming. A clean architecture is not only about where source files live; it also needs to produce sane HTML.

Layer 4: PageRegionContent is the region dispatcher

The region dispatcher is where a normalized PageRegion becomes a real pattern. Its discriminated union currently supports regions such as page headers, heroes, articles, reviews, cards, CTAs, collections, archives, galleries, readers, details, profiles, tables of contents, advertisements, and nested groups.

The useful property here is that each region type is explicit. A region with component: "article" carries PArticleProps; a cards region carries PCardProps; a gallery region carries PGalleryProps. TypeScript can therefore connect the composition contract to the actual pattern contract.

This removes a common page-builder smell: a generic props: Record<string, unknown> object that is passed into whatever component name happens to be stored in content.

Nested groups are composition, not a new component layer

The group region is also important because it can divide nested regions into main and aside placements. If aside regions exist, the dispatcher uses LSidebar; otherwise it renders the main regions directly.

This lets an article page combine author information, a table of contents, related articles, a newsletter, the editorial header, and the article body without inventing a one-off ‘BlogDetailLayout’ component that duplicates sidebar logic.

At the same time, the group does not become a generic recursive page builder with unlimited arbitrary nesting. It still works with the same approved PageRegion union.

Layer 5: Project patterns own reusable product behavior

The P* layer contains reusable patterns that are larger than a primitive component but smaller than a full page. This is where behavior such as card collections, galleries, archives, page headers, readers, CTAs, post navigation, filters, and advertisements belongs.

The distinction matters because a Project pattern can own control flow.

PCard, for example, owns a card collection. Its collection template decides whether items render as a grid, list-like arrangement, slider, mosaic, asymmetric layout, showcase, or another approved collection form. The selected item renderer, CCard, renders one card.

That separation prevents page partials from repeatedly writing the same card loop, and it prevents a single card component from pretending it also owns the layout of every collection in which it appears.

The next article in this series will go deeper into this exact ownership question: where should the loop actually live?

Layer 6: Components render smaller UI contracts

The C* layer contains smaller reusable UI units: buttons, links, headings, images, metadata, columns, rows, tags, tabs, progress indicators, selects, and the single-item card renderer.

This layer should be reusable without knowing which page it is on. A button should not know that it is inside a project detail page. A metadata item should not know that it is inside a blog card. A grid item should not fetch content.

That sounds obvious, but it becomes difficult when a site grows. ‘Convenient’ props often pull business context downward. A card starts checking the current route. A link starts deciding analytics categories. A heading starts reading CMS state. Each shortcut makes one file easier today while weakening the ownership boundary.

The architecture tries to push contextual decisions upward and keep rendering decisions downward.

Layer 7: Layouts own geometry

The L* layer exists so spacing and structural geometry do not leak into every Project pattern.

LPage, LSection, and LSidebar answer different structural questions. A page pattern can use them without redefining site containers, section spacing, or sidebar behavior.

This also makes responsive audits easier. When a wide layout feels wrong, I can inspect the layout owner first instead of searching through every content pattern for duplicated width classes.

Tailwind remains the styling standard. The architecture does not require every spacing value or class combination to become a custom token. The important rule is ownership and consistency: structural layout decisions should live where structural layout is owned.

Scripts are progressive enhancement, not the page runtime

Astro components render HTML without a client-side runtime by default. Folio X keeps that characteristic instead of treating Astro as a shell around a large JavaScript application.

The site has a central main.ts initializer, but feature scripts are loaded conditionally. Image-gallery code is imported only when a gallery marker exists. Article TOC behavior is imported only when a TOC exists. Archive filtering, collection filtering, product filtering, reader behavior, and slider behavior follow the same pattern.

That does two useful things.

  1. HTML remains the primary output and can be useful before feature code runs.
  2. Feature-specific JavaScript does not need to be eagerly loaded on pages that cannot use it.

I still keep a small set of core initializers for features that are site-wide, such as the header, loading screen, scroll progress, scroll-to-top behavior, dialogs, selects, and reveal behavior. The boundary is pragmatic rather than ideological: global behavior can be global; feature behavior should be conditional.

Why the dependency direction matters

The architecture becomes easier to reason about when dependencies mostly point downward:

CMS / content
      ↓
page data + composition
      ↓
PPage / page regions
      ↓
Project patterns
      ↓
Components + Layouts
      ↓
HTML
      ↓
optional feature scripts

The dangerous direction is the reverse. If a low-level component starts importing page data, or a layout starts fetching a CMS collection, the boundary becomes circular in practice even if imports still compile.

This is why I care more about ownership than naming conventions. Prefixes such as L*, C*, and P* are useful because they make ownership visible, but the prefixes are not the architecture by themselves. A poorly scoped PWhatever remains poorly scoped.

What I gained from this structure

I do not have a clean before-and-after productivity metric for this architecture, so I will not invent one. The benefits I can support from the source are structural.

New content types fit into existing boundaries

The same page-region system supports products, labs, projects, blog posts, publications, readers, and system states. They do not all share the same page template, but they share the same composition vocabulary.

CMS changes do not automatically become UI API changes

Because PageBuilder adapts content into application contracts, the CMS representation and component API do not have to be identical. That gives me room to keep editor-facing values understandable while keeping component-facing values precise.

Reusable patterns can own their real control flow

Collections, galleries, archives, readers, and other patterns can own their internal loops and behavior instead of making every page duplicate them.

Rendered HTML stays a first-class output

Because client behavior is additive, the architecture still works with Astro’s server/build-time rendering model instead of assuming every interaction needs a hydrated framework component.

The trade-offs

This structure is not free.

The first trade-off is more contracts. A content field may have a schema type, a normalized page-region type, a Project prop type, and a Component prop type. For a tiny site, that can feel excessive.

The second trade-off is that the page builder becomes an important integration point. It has to know how CMS values map to sources and Project patterns. If it becomes a dumping ground for unrelated business logic, the architecture degrades quickly.

The third trade-off is intentional constraint. Editors cannot assemble arbitrary components in arbitrary combinations. That is a feature for this portfolio because visual consistency and code ownership matter more than unlimited layout freedom. It would not automatically be the right decision for a general-purpose website builder.

The fourth trade-off is migration cost. Once content and code are separated by explicit contracts, changing a contract requires updating schema, data, mapper, type, and renderer together. That is more work than silently accepting any object shape, but it also makes the change visible and testable.

Rules I use when adding a new feature

When I add a feature now, I do not begin by asking ‘which folder should this file go in?’ I ask a sequence of ownership questions.

  1. Is this page-specific composition? It belongs under src/components/pages/<page>/.
  2. Is this a reusable product-level pattern? It belongs in the P* layer.
  3. Is this one smaller reusable UI unit? It belongs in the C* layer.
  4. Is this structural geometry? It belongs in the L* layer.
  5. Does the CMS need to edit it? Add only the data fields and approved choices the editor actually needs.
  6. Does content need normalization? Map it before it reaches the rendering pattern.
  7. Does it need browser behavior? Keep the HTML useful first, then initialize the feature only where the relevant DOM exists.

Those questions are more stable than any exact folder tree because they describe responsibility rather than file placement.

How this differs from a generic Astro starter

Astro itself does not require this architecture. Its component model is deliberately flexible: an Astro component can be a small reusable fragment, a page layout, or an entire page. Content collections can load structured content and validate it with schemas. Those primitives give the project freedom.

The architecture described here is the additional discipline I added on top of those primitives.

Astro gives me components. Folio X decides which components are Layouts, Components, Projects, or page composition.

Astro gives me content collections. Folio X decides that CMS data must pass through application contracts rather than directly naming arbitrary renderers.

Astro gives me scripts and framework integrations. Folio X decides that feature scripts should be conditional and additive unless a feature genuinely needs more.

That distinction is important. Framework capability is not the same thing as application architecture.

What I would change if the project grew much larger

If Folio X became a multi-team product, I would probably split some of the current page-builder responsibilities into smaller typed resolvers. The source already contains focused page-data functions for several detail and catalog pages, so there is a natural path toward more explicit feature modules if the integration surface keeps growing.

I would also formalize contract tests around the highest-value CMS mappings. The current build and schema validation catch many shape errors, but a larger editorial team would benefit from tests that assert specific content configurations map to specific region contracts.

What I would not change first is the layer direction. Even if the folders were reorganized, I would keep content, composition, Project patterns, Components, Layouts, and enhancement as separate responsibilities.

The main lesson: architecture is ownership

The biggest change in this portfolio was not moving files into prettier folders. It was deciding which layer is allowed to make which decision.

Content can describe content. Composition can translate content into page regions. Page templates can own page structure. Project patterns can own reusable control flow. Components can render smaller UI contracts. Layouts can own geometry. Scripts can enhance the HTML when the feature exists.

Once those boundaries became explicit, architecture reviews became easier because I could ask a concrete question: is this decision being made by the layer that owns it?

That question has also influenced the production systems I work on outside this portfolio. In the previous case study, centralizing e-commerce promotion work improved the workflow because one business operation gained a clear owner. The same principle appears here at a different scale: software becomes easier to evolve when responsibilities have clear owners.

The next article will narrow this architecture down to one deceptively small question: when a card pattern renders a collection, where should the loop actually live?
